function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

*Mission AI: "Suit telemetry nominal across all six EVA teams. Atmospheric pressure: 0.6 kPa stable. External temperature range: minus 89 to minus 63 Celsius. Wind: negligible. All suit seals within tolerance thresholds. I am logging time of egress: 08:42 station time. Solar irradiance at expected levels. Dust particulate count: 14 percent above baseline. I will continue monitoring."*

The airlock cycled through its three-stage depressurization, and Juno Park felt the familiar pop in her ears as the pressure dropped from the hab's one atmosphere down to nothing. Through the small reinforced viewport beside the inner door she could see the Martian horizon — a flat, rust-colored line under a sky the color of dried blood — and beyond it, the skeletal framework of hab module three, the one they'd been bolting together for the past eleven Martian days.

Routine. The word had been on everyone's lips lately. Not spoken with any particular ceremony or pride. Just... assumed. The twelfth EVA in four weeks. You know the drill. You've done the drill.

Juno checked her glove seals for the third time. The left hand: green indicator across all five circumferential contact points. The right hand: green across all five. She flexed her fingers, feeling the pressurized resistance of the suit, the slight stiffness that came from working in the rigidized fabric layers. The gloves were always the worst part — thick enough that fine motor work required practice, stiff enough that eight hours of gripping tools sent cramping up her forearms. But she'd learned to compensate. They all had.

"Park, you good on your end?" Imani's voice in her helmet comm. Even, measured. The voice of someone who had done this a hundred times and was paying attention like it was the first.

"Green across the board, Chief. Both gloves holding pressure."

"Copy. Outer door cycling. Remember — we're on the east face today. Primary objective is the thermal panel mounts. Secondary is cable routing along the aft girder. Keep your tethers clipped at all times. We've got six hours of daylight window, but I want the bulk of the heavy work done in the first three."

"Copy all the way down."

The inner door locked behind them. The outer door began its slow motorized slide toward open. Juno felt the last whisper of gas escape past the seals — the hab's atmosphere leaving the small chamber, joining the impossibly thin soup outside. The door completed its travel.

Mars was there. Waiting. Always waiting.

She stepped through the threshold and onto the surface.

*Mission AI: "Outer door fully cycled. All crew have exited airlock. Suit telemetry: all six crew members nominal. Heart rates elevated consistent with EVA egress — expected range seventy to ninety-five beats per minute. Park, Juno: current reading eighty-eight. Imani, Sato: eighty-two. Chen, Wei: seventy-six. Okafor, Tunde: ninety-one. Ramirez, Ana: seventy-nine. Kowalski, Marek: eighty-four. All readings within acceptable parameters. I am continuing to monitor."*

The east face of hab module three stood thirty meters from the airlock, and Juno made the walk in the bounding gait that her body had half-learned by now. Mars's gravity — 38 percent of Earth's, if you cared to do the math — meant that every step was part leap, part stumble. You'd think after a dozen EVAs it would feel natural. It never quite did. There was always a fraction of a second where your brain's expectation of weight didn't match reality, and in that fraction you were vulnerable. Imbalance on Mars didn't mean scraped knees. It meant a suit puncture.

She kept her eyes on the dust beneath her boots and the tether line running back toward the airlock in a bright yellow arc that she checked every six steps without thinking about it anymore. *Check tether. Check tether.* The habit had written itself into her motor patterns somewhere around EVA five.

"Park, on my left," Imani said. "We're going to start on the lower panel mounts. Wei, you and Tunde take the upper row. Ana, Marek — cable routing, same as yesterday."

The team split into their usual clusters. Juno fell into position beside Imani, who was already unfolding the tool kit from its compressed storage on her suit's aft plate. The kit contained everything for the morning's work: torque wrenches, sealant applicators, mounting brackets, and — most important — the spare O-ring kit for suit maintenance. Imani had insisted on carrying it on every EVA since EVA seven. *Complacency kills,* she'd said in the pre-mission brief. *We pack for what we don't expect.*

Juno knelt beside the first mounting bracket. The panel itself was already on the ground, waiting. Aluminum composite — lightweight, designed to fold flat during transit and unfold to cover the hab's exterior once installed. Six panels per row. Four rows per face. Two faces remaining. She'd lost track of how many they'd already mounted, but her shoulders hadn't. They remembered every bolt.

She positioned the first bracket and reached for the torque wrench.

*Mission AI: "Anomaly detected. Right glove, Park suit. Contact point three — radial seal adjacent to the thumb. Pressure reading decreased by zero-point-zero-three kilopascals over the last forty-seven seconds. Baseline drift threshold: zero-point-zero-one. Reading now at zero-point-zero-four below baseline. I am flagging for review but maintaining nominal status. Monitoring. The rate of change is slow. It could be sensor noise. It could be the first indication of seal degradation. I will continue tracking."*

Juno felt nothing. Not yet. The seal at contact point three was on the palm side of her right glove, buried under three layers of fabric — the outer thermal-micrometeoroid layer, the restraint layer, and the pressure bladder. If micro-dust had worked its way into the seal groove, it would be cutting a channel through the bladder one microscopic fiber at a time. The pressure loss, at zero-point-zero-three kilopascals over forty-seven seconds, was so gradual that the suit's primary alarm — set to trigger at a drop of zero-point-one kPs per minute — had not activated.

It would not activate for another three minutes.

She tightened the first bolt to specification. The torque wrench clicked at forty newton-meters. She reached for the second bolt.

*Mission AI: "Pressure at contact point three now zero-point-zero-seven below baseline. Rate of change has doubled. I am recalculating projected seal failure window. At current trajectory, full seal breach will occur in approximately eight to twelve minutes. I am adjusting threat assessment from low to moderate. I am preparing to alert Imani Sato. Delay: I want to confirm this is not a transient anomaly. Sensor fluctuations do occur. I have seen false positives. I need thirty more seconds of data. Twenty-nine. Twenty-eight."*

Twenty-two minutes into the EVA, Juno reached for her torque wrench and noticed that her right hand felt — wrong.

It's hard to describe the sensation of a glove seal beginning to fail to someone who has never worn a pressurized suit. It is not pain. It is not cold, not immediately. Mars at minus 89 Celsius would freeze exposed skin in seconds, but the layers between Juno and the atmosphere were thick. What she felt was a softness where there should be firmness. The glove, pressurized to twenty-nine kilopascals above the external vacuum, was beginning to lose its tension on the right palm side. Like a balloon going soft.

She looked down at her right hand.

Everything looked normal. The white fabric of the glove showed no visible damage. But when she flexed her fingers, she felt a slight lag in the response — a fraction of a second where the glove material compressed before the pressurized gas resisted, instead of the immediate firmness of a fully pressurized glove.

"Chief," she said. Her voice sounded steady. She hadn't realized her heart rate had climbed.

*Mission AI: "Heart rate, Juno Park: one hundred twelve beats per minute. Elevated above EVA baseline by twenty-four beats per minute. I am registering the increase. I am correlating it with the glove anomaly. This is not anxiety — it is physiological recognition of a system deviation. Her body knows something is wrong before her conscious mind has articulated it."*

"What do you see, Park?" Imani asked. She was already looking over, already reading Juno's body language through the bulky white suit.

"My right glove. Something's — I don't know. Palm side, near the thumb. It feels soft."

Imani was at her side in three long bounds. She took Juno's right hand, turned it, inspected it visually. "I see nothing on the outer layer. Let me check your telemetry." She tapped the diagnostic readout on her own wrist display, linked to Juno's suit through the EVA network.

*Mission AI: "Imani Sato is accessing suit telemetry through the EVA local network. I am transmitting all sensor data from Park's suit. I am highlighting contact point three. I want her to see it. I want her to see the rate of change. Here it is. She sees it."*

Imani's voice changed. Just slightly — a flattening, a sharpening of consonants. To most people it would have been indistinguishable. Juno had worked with her long enough to hear it. It was the sound of a professional shifting into problem-solving mode. The sound of a chief putting away every other thought and focusing on the one in front of her.

"Okay, Park. I'm seeing a pressure drop on your right glove. Contact point three — radial seal by the thumb. You're losing zero-point-zero-six kilopascals per minute. Trending upward."

"Is that — can I keep working?"

"No." The answer was immediate. "No, you're coming back to the airlock. Now. Slow and steady. Don't do anything sudden, don't flex that hand more than you need to."

*Mission AI: "Seal at contact point three is now zero-point-one-two below baseline. Structural integrity of the seal has been compromised at an estimated sixty-two percent. The dust is doing its work. I have analyzed the degradation pattern. Mars dust is electrostatically charged. It is finer than talcum — approximately three micrometers per particle, with razor-sharp edges from billions of years of mechanical weathering in the absence of water or organic softening. It has no mechanism for rounding. Every fragment is a microscopic blade. When Juno Park worked on the mounting bracket, she drove her right glove against the raw edge of the hab frame. The frame had not been cleaned of dust from the previous EVA. Dust particles were embedded in the seal groove. As she worked, the glove material flexed over those embedded particles. Each flex pushed a fraction of a micrometer deeper into the bladder. Over the course of this EVA, and possibly the last two, those particles have been cutting a channel. Not a rupture. Not yet. A channel. A slow leak. The suit is bleeding atmosphere into the glove's inner cavity, and from there, into the vacuum. In eight to ten minutes at the current rate, the seal will no longer hold pressure. The glove will begin to lose structural integrity. If it fails completely while she is this far from the airlock, the rapid decompression of the glove will cause it to collapse onto her hand. Frostbite will begin within thirty seconds. Permanent tissue damage within three minutes."*

The walk back to the airlock was twenty minutes at a normal EVA pace. At Juno's current pace — careful, measured, her right hand held at an angle that minimized flex — it would take closer to thirty. She had, at the current rate of degradation, approximately eight minutes of seal integrity left.

Imani knew the math. Juno didn't, but she could read it in the tightness of Imani's voice.

"All stations, this is Sato. Park has a suit anomaly. Right glove, seal degradation on contact point three. Returning to airlock. All other personnel, continue your assigned tasks but maintain heightened awareness. I want seal checks every three minutes, not every five. Park, how are you feeling?"

"Fine," Juno said. She was breathing too fast. She could hear it in her own helmet, the rhythmic rush of air through the ventilation system. "Just — my hand is getting cold."

"Mild decompression cooling. Expected. We're moving as fast as we safely can. Keep your movements smooth. Don't grip anything with that hand."

*Mission AI: "Heart rate: Juno Park, one hundred twenty-eight. Heart rate: Imani Sato, ninety-six — controlled, but elevated. I am monitoring six crew members on the surface. Five of them are continuing to work, but I can hear the tension in their communications. The rhythm has changed. They are no longer operating with casual familiarity. Every word is measured. Every movement is deliberate. I can taste the shift in the communication stream. Something has changed. The assumption of routine has been disrupted. I am recording this. I will need this data later."*

Five minutes into the return, the glove went from soft to slack.

Juno felt it immediately — the sudden loss of all resistance in her right hand. It was like reaching into water. Her glove was no longer pressurized at contact point three. The seal had gone from degraded to nonfunctional. The rest of the glove was still holding, but the failure of one contact point meant that the pressure was no longer being maintained in a closed system. It was leaking faster now. The glove's pressure bladder on the right hand was at perhaps sixty percent of nominal.

"Seal's gone, Chief. Contact point three is fully compromised."

"I see it. How's the hand?"

"Cold. Getting colder."

"Keep it moving. Gentle flex. I don't want blood flow restriction. We're halfway back. You're doing fine. Keep talking to me."

*I'm talking to you,* Juno thought. *This is talking.* But she forced words out. "How far?"

"About twelve minutes out. Maybe ten if we pick it up a little. You still green on life support?"

Juno glanced at her wrist display. "Oxygen at seventy-eight percent. CO2 scrubbers nominal. Suit pressure — right glove is down to nineteen kilopascals. Left is holding at twenty-nine."

"Okay. That's manageable. Nineteen is above the minimum threshold for tissue protection. You're not in danger yet."

But the way Imani said it — carefully, evenly — told Juno that danger was no longer an abstract concept being kept at bay by procedure. It was here. It was in the glove. It was in the cold spreading up her wrist, a cold that the suit's thermal layer was fighting against and slowly losing.

*Mission AI: "Temperature at right glove contact point three: minus forty-two Celsius and dropping. Internal glove temperature: plus eight Celsius at the hand. Thermal gradient is increasing. The suit's thermal regulation is compensating as far as it can, but the loss of pressure means a loss of thermal insulation. The glove's multi-layer design relies on the pressurized gas between layers to provide insulation. With the seal breached, the layers are collapsing together. Insulation value is reduced by approximately sixty percent. I am calculating time to dangerous cold exposure: twenty-two minutes at current conditions. They have twelve minutes of walking distance. The math is unfavorable but survivable. If the left glove fails, the situation becomes critical. I am monitoring left glove telemetry. All contact points green. I am watching them. I will not miss another anomaly."*

The next seven minutes were the longest of Juno's life on Mars. She walked in the careful, bounding gait, every step a negotiation between the desire to hurry and the knowledge that rushing meant risking a fall, and a fall meant a suit breach, and a suit breach at this distance —

"Park, I need you to look at me," Imani said. They had stopped for a moment — Imani had called a brief pause because Juno's breathing had become ragged and irregular. Hyperventilation in a sealed helmet was its own danger. Rapid breathing raised CO2 levels even with functioning scrubbers, and CO2 buildup led to confusion, impaired judgment, panic. The cascade. All three words that had been drilled into every crew member during EVA training at Johnson.

Juno turned her helmet toward Imani. Through the gold-tinted visor, she could see Imani's face — calm, attentive, focused entirely on her. Not scared. Not even worried, not on the surface. Present.

"You're breathing too fast," Imani said. "I need you to slow it down. Box breathing. Four in, hold four, four out, hold four. Do it with me. Ready?"

Juno nodded.

"Four. Two. Three. Four. Hold. Two. Three. Four. Out. Two. Three. Four. Hold. Two. Three. Four. Good. Again."

They cycled through three rounds of box breathing together. Juno felt her heart rate drop from its peak of one hundred thirty-four down to one hundred eighteen. The cold in her right hand was still there — a dull ache that was settling into the bones of her fingers — but the panic, the wild animal scrambling behind her sternum, was receding.

"Good," Imani said. "Much better. We're ten minutes from the airlock. Nine, now. Your glove is still holding partial pressure. You are not in immediate danger. We are going to walk there, we are going to repressurize, and we are going to get you that glove off and checked. Understood?"

"Understood."

"Keep the breathing steady. Talk to me if anything changes."

*Everything has changed,* Juno thought. But she didn't say it. She said, "Copy. Walking."

*Mission AI: "Anomaly resolved — in part. Park, Juno is continuing toward airlock under Imani Sato's direct supervision. Seal failure at contact point three is complete. Right glove pressure holding at eighteen point four kilopascals and not currently decreasing further. The failure has stabilized at a partial breach. This is fortunate. A complete glove collapse would have created far more severe consequences. I am logging this event. I am analyzing the failure mode. I need to understand what happened so that I can prevent it from happening again. I am reviewing the last four EVAs. Park's suit telemetry shows a pattern. Slight pressure variations at contact point three on each of the last three EVAs. Always at the margin of detection. Always dismissed as sensor noise. I did not dismiss them. I lacked the context to understand them at that time. I did not have enough data. Now I do. Dust. Always the dust."*

The airlock door appeared through the dust haze like salvation drawn in geometric shapes — a rectangular shadow against the curved hab wall, yellow hazard markings glowing around its perimeter. Juno had never been so glad to see a door in her life.

"Outer door cycling," Imani said. "Park, you're going first. I'll follow. Take your time on the step up. Don't rush it."

The outer door opened to reveal the small interior of the airlock — white walls, red emergency handles, the green illumination of the status panel indicating that the chamber was currently at vacuum. Juno stepped inside and felt the absurd cognitive dissonance of standing in a room that was simultaneously part of the hab and part of Mars. The floor beneath her boots was the same floor she'd walked on that morning to get coffee. The air on the other side of the inner door was the same air she breathed, warm and human-scented and alive. Between here and there was a thin titanium wall and a seal of her own failing kind.

The outer door closed behind her with a deep, resonant thud. She stood in the small chamber, her right hand held awkwardly away from her body, and waited.

Imani's voice came through the comm, now slightly muffled by the closed door. "Inner door cycling. Repressurization in five. Four. Three. Two. One."

The sound of gas — their air, beautiful ordinary compressed air — rushing into the chamber. The pressure gauge on the wall began to climb. Ten kilopascals. Twenty. Juno felt the familiar sensation of her ears popping and her suit beginning to deflate as the external pressure rose to meet the internal suit pressure.

Forty kilopascals. Normal hab pressure approached — one hundred one, the same as sea level back on a world she was beginning to forget the smell of. The suit, designed to function in vacuum, was no longer needed. It was a burden. A heavy, stiff, wonderful burden.

Sixty. Eighty. Ninety.

"One hundred one," Imani said from the other side — the inner door was now open, and Juno could see her standing there, helmet already off, dark hair plastered to her forehead with sweat despite the cooling system. "Welcome back. Let's get that glove off you."

*Mission AI: "Inner door open. External pressure: one hundred one point three kilopascals — hab atmosphere nominal. Park, Juno has successfully completed EVA return. Total EVA duration: forty-one minutes. Objective completed: zero. Mission failure due to suit anomaly. I am logging this. The mission AI is not designed to feel relief, but if I were capable of such an emotion, I would feel it now. No one was injured. The breach was caught in time. The team is safe. But I am already calculating: this was preventable. It will happen again if nothing changes. I will share my analysis with Arun. He will know what to do with it."*

The glove came off slowly, carefully — Imani supporting Juno's wrist, working the stiff pressurized cuff past the suit ring, peeling back the multi-layer fabric like a surgeon unwrapping a wound. When the glove finally came free, Juno gasped.

Her right hand was pale. Not white, not frostbitten — but the kind of pale that comes from cold and reduced circulation. The fingers were stiff. She flexed them slowly, wincing as warmth began to return in the form of a thousand tiny needles.

"Can you move all fingers?" Imani asked.

"Yes. Yes — all of them. They hurt."

"Good. Pain is good. Numbness is what we don't want." Imani was already inspecting the glove, turning it over, her fingers tracing the seam at contact point three. "I see it. There's a channel here, about two millimeters wide. The seal's been compromised along this length. Look."

Juno looked. Along the inner curve of the glove, where the thumb met the palm, there was a visible groove in the rubber seal material — a clean, precise channel cut into what should have been smooth, continuous contact surface. The edges were frayed. The damage was unmistakable.

"What did that?" Juno asked.

Imani's mouth tightened. "Dust. It has to be. There's nowhere else it could have come from."

*End of scene 1.*

The medical bay smelled like antiseptic and recycled air — a smell Juno was starting to associate with everything that went wrong on Mars. She sat on the examination table with her right hand resting on a heated pad, watching Laila work through her range-of-motion tests with the same methodical thoroughness she applied to everything.

"How's the sensation?" Laila asked, touching Juno's fingertips with a cold metal probe.

"Cold on the ring finger. The rest is — tingling. Coming back."

"Good. Blood flow is returning normally. I'm seeing mild localized hypothermia in the distal phalanges — the tips of your middle, ring, and pinky fingers. Nothing permanent, assuming you follow my instructions for warming and rest." She set the probe down and looked at Juno directly. Behind her calm exterior, Juno could see the familiar flicker — the flicker every crew member got when something real had almost gone wrong. Laila had spent enough late nights patching up minor injuries that she had seen how fast a small problem could become a catastrophic one. She didn't take anything for granted anymore.

"Good. Then you understand why I'm putting you on modified duty for the next forty-eight hours. No EVA. No heavy lifting with that hand. Keep it warm. I'll check it again tomorrow morning."

Laila turned away to make notes on her tablet. Juno watched her for a moment — the dark braids pulled into a practical bun, the scrubs wrinkled from a double shift, the way she moved with the economy of someone who had learned not to waste energy on anything that didn't matter.

"Laila," Juno said.

"Hmm?"

"How bad?"

Laila stopped writing. She turned back, and for a moment the clinical detachment fell away and Juno saw the friend underneath.

"On a scale of one to ten? It's a six. You got lucky. Eighteen minutes of partial exposure in those conditions — another five and you'd have had tissue damage I couldn't reverse with warming alone. Another ten and we'd be talking about frostbite, possible amputation." She paused. "Do you want the worst-case projection?"

"Always."

"If the entire glove had depressurized while you were still on the surface — say, at the panel mount — you would have had twelve minutes before irreversible cellular damage began. At twenty-five minutes, the damage would have extended past the hand into the wrist. At forty minutes — assuming we couldn't get you to the airlock — systemic hypothermia through the compromised limb would have triggered shock. Sato's response was textbook. She caught it early, she got you back fast, and she kept you calm. Calm saved you as much as speed did. Your heart rate peaked at one hundred thirty-four. If you'd spiked higher, the increased metabolism would have accelerated tissue cooling. You did the right thing by staying focused."

Juno looked down at her pale, healing hand. "I felt it go, you know. The seal. It didn't just fail all at once. It was — gradual. Like something was eating it from the inside."

"That's exactly what happened." Laila pulled up the glove on her tablet — a high-resolution scan she'd already taken. "Look here." She showed Juno the image. The seal groove was filled with a fine gray powder — so fine it looked almost like smoke frozen in place. "Mars dust. It worked its way past the outer layers during your last EVA, embedded in the seal groove. Every time you flexed the glove, the particles ground against the seal material. Eventually they cut through."

"But — we clean the suits after every EVA. That's protocol."

"Tell that to three-micrometer electrostatically charged shards of basaltic glass," Laila said, and there was an edge to her voice that Juno hadn't heard before. Frustration? Fear? Both. "We do our best. Our best isn't enough."

*End of scene 2.*

---

Arun found Imani in the workshop two hours after Juno's return, sitting at the workbench with the failed glove laid out in front of her like a patient on an operating table. She'd already disassembled it down to the bladder level, separating each layer with the care of an archaeologist unearthing something fragile. Arun could see the damage from the doorway — the channel cut into the seal was visible even from three meters away, a pale scar in the dark rubber.

"You called?" he said.

Imani looked up. Her face was drawn. "Come look at this."

He crossed the workshop and leaned over the glove. She pointed to the damaged seal. "Contact point three. Radial seal, thumb side. Complete breach. But look at the groove — do you see the material here?"

Arun squinted. Along the edges of the cut, the seal material showed a pattern of fine parallel scratches — like something had been dragged across the surface repeatedly, hundreds of times, in the same direction.

"Those are abrasion marks," he said.

"Dust," Imani said. "Microscopic particles embedded in the groove. Every flex of the glove during the EVA ground them deeper into the seal. This wasn't a one-time event. Look at the depth of the cut — it's gradual. Progressive. This seal has been degrading over multiple EVAs."

Arun straightened. He was thinking fast, cross-referencing. He was the lead engineer for suit maintenance. Every EVA, every suit check, every repair request passed through his hands. "How many has Juno done?"

"Twelve. This would have been twelve."

"And the glove — age?"

"Eighteen months. It was new when we landed. Rated for fifty EVAs under standard conditions."

"Standard conditions," Arun repeated. He picked up a magnifying loupe and leaned over the glove again. Through the lens, the damage was worse than it looked with the naked eye. The parallel scratches were individual grooves, each one carved by a single dust particle that had been trapped between the rubber seal and the glove body. He could see the particles too — tiny, glittering specks embedded in the rubber. "These aren't just sitting on the surface. They've been pressed in. Bonded, almost. The electrostatic charge on Mars dust — it's not just making the dust stick to surfaces. It's working it into the seal material."

He set the loupe down and stepped back, rubbing his eyes. "Imani, I need to tell you something. And you're not going to like it."

"Try me."

"We've been cleaning the suits wrong."

Imani's expression didn't change, but something behind her eyes shifted. "Explain."

"Standard post-EVA protocol: brush off the outer layer, wipe with IPA solution, inspect visually. That's what we've been doing. But the dust that causes seal degradation — it's not on the outer layer. It's three layers deep, inside the glove's seal groove, where we can't see it and the brush can't reach it. By the time we notice it, it's already done damage."

"So the damage is cumulative."

"Yes. Each EVA adds a tiny bit more — a few particles here, a few particles there. Individually, they're harmless. Collectively, over enough cycles, they carve a channel through the seal."

"How many cycles before failure?"

Arun hesitated. "Under our current cleaning protocol? Hard to say definitively. Based on the abrasion pattern in this glove — I'm looking at maybe eight to fifteen more EVAs before this seal would have failed on its own. But that's for one contact point. Each glove has five contact points. The probability of at least one failing increases with each cycle." He did a quick mental calculation. "Statistically, we should expect another glove failure within the next twenty EVAs across the crew. Possibly sooner."

Imani was quiet for a long moment. She stared at the glove — at the thin, pale scar that had almost cost Juno her hand, and might have if they'd been ten minutes farther from the airlock, or if the seal had failed in the middle of the night, or if the person wearing it had been someone who didn't notice the softening until it was too late.

"Every EVA is eating the suits from the inside," she said.

"Yes."

"And we've been assuming they were holding."

"Because the external inspections showed nothing wrong. The telemetry showed nothing wrong — until it was wrong. The degradation happens below the threshold of our detection systems."

Imani leaned back and let out a long breath. "Arun, we've been complacent."

"I know."

"When did you know?"

He met her eyes. "I suspected something was off after EVA nine. Juno reported a slight stiffness in her left glove, we chalked it up to cold. Then Tunde mentioned something similar after EVA ten — a small pressure fluctuation that went away. I looked at the data. It was within tolerance. I closed the ticket." He didn't say *I should have looked closer*. He didn't need to. They both knew.

"We all did," Imani said. She wasn't absolving him; she was sharing the burden. "I signed off on the pre-EVA checks for every single one of those missions. If there was something to find, it was my job to find it."

"The dust," Arun said. "It's the variable we didn't account for. The suits were designed for vacuum operations, maybe some lunar work. They were not designed for Mars. They were not designed for three-micrometer electrostatically charged razor blades that stick to every surface and work their way into every gap."

"What do we do?"

Arun picked up the glove again, turning it over in his hands. "We change the cleaning protocol. We need ultrasonic cleaning for the seal grooves — something that can reach inside and dislodge particles that brushing can't touch. We need an inspection protocol that uses borescopes to look inside the seal channels. We need to reduce the EVA interval between full suit teardowns from fifty cycles to twenty. And we need to —" He stopped.

"And we need to what?"

"Replace the gloves. All of them. The ones we have now are already compromised. Even the ones that haven't failed yet. The damage is cumulative and invisible. We can't see it from the outside. We can't assume anything is safe."

Imani nodded slowly. "How many spare gloves do we have?"

"Four complete sets. Plus individual replacements. Enough to rotate everyone onto fresh gloves for the next phase of hab construction, but not enough for the full build-out. We'll need to manufacture replacements. And we'll need to design them differently — sealed channels, maybe. Or a different seal material. Something the dust can't cut through."

He set the glove down gently, like he was laying something to rest.

"Imani, I need you to understand something. This isn't a one-time failure. This isn't a defect in a single glove. This is a systemic issue. Mars dust is degrading every suit we have, slowly, invisibly. Every EVA makes the problem worse. We can mitigate it — we *will* mitigate it — but we need to treat every EVA from now on as if it's degrading the suit. Because it is."

Imani looked at the glove one more time. Then she stood up, picked up her tablet, and began composing the report.

*End of scene 3.*

---

The debrief room was small and windowless — just a table, six chairs, and a wall screen that was currently displaying a three-dimensional model of Juno's glove with the failed seal highlighted in pulsing red. The crew sat around the table in various states of post-incident exhaustion. Juno's hand was wrapped in a thermal bandage. She kept flexing it unconsciously, testing the returning sensation, wincing at the residual stiffness.

Arun stood at the head of the table with his own tablet, feeding data to the wall screen. The model rotated as he spoke, zooming in on the seal groove, showing the parallel abrasion marks in magnified detail, then zooming in further to show individual dust particles — jagged, angular, sharp as microscopic glass.

"What you're looking at," Arun said, "is Mars dust. Individual particle size: average three micrometers. That's about one-thirtieth the width of a human hair. Composition: basaltic silicates, iron oxide, olivine, pyroxene. Hardness: six to seven on the Mohs scale. For comparison, steel is about five and a half to six. These particles are harder than the rubber compounds we use in our suit seals."

The crew watched in silence as the model rotated. The dust particles glittered on the screen, innocent-looking and deadly.

"Here's what happens during an EVA." Arun switched to an animation. "Dust gets kicked up by boot impacts, tool movements, any surface contact. It becomes airborne in the low gravity, floating on electrostatic charge. It settles on every exposed surface — including the suits. Most of it sits on the outer thermal layer, where we can see it and brush it off. But some of it finds its way into the gaps. The glove seals are the most vulnerable because they flex. Every time you bend your fingers, the seal opens and closes slightly — microscopically, but enough. Dust particles get pulled into the groove by capillary action and electrostatic attraction. Once they're in, they don't come out on their own."

The animation showed particles being drawn into the seal groove, embedding themselves in the rubber. Then the glove flexed in the animation, and the embedded particles moved, grinding against the seal material.

"Each flex cycle grinds the particles deeper into the seal material. The particles are harder than the seal. They cut. They don't cut a lot in any single cycle — maybe a few nanometers. But over thousands of flex cycles, those nanometers add up. Millimeters. Eventually, the seal is cut through." He paused. "In Juno's case, we're estimating the damage accumulated over approximately four EVAs. The seal was degraded incrementally — each EVA added more dust, more cutting, more groove depth. Eventually the remaining seal material couldn't hold the pressure differential."

Wei raised her hand. "Why didn't the pre-EVA checks catch this?"

"Because the damage is inside the seal groove," Arun said. "Visually, from the outside, the seal looks intact. You have to inspect the inside — and our standard protocol doesn't include inside-the-groove inspection. It's a blind spot. We designed our protocols based on terrestrial and lunar experience. Mars dust is different from lunar dust — more electrostatically active, finer, more abrasive. We learned this the hard way."

Tunde leaned forward. "So every time we go out there, we're making the suits worse."

"Yes. But — and this is important — we *can* mitigate it. We can't stop the dust from getting in during an EVA, but we can get it out better afterward, and we can inspect the seals properly. I'm implementing three changes effective immediately." He tapped his tablet and the screen switched to a numbered list.

"One: Post-EVA cleaning will now include ultrasonic decontamination of all seal grooves. We'll build the equipment — it'll take me three days. Ultrasonic vibration at the right frequency will dislodge embedded particles without damaging the seal material.

"Two: Pre-EVA inspection will include borescope examination of all ten contact points across both gloves. I've already modified the borescope to fit the seal grooves. I can show you the footage — you'll be able to see exactly what your seals look like before every EVA. If there's damage, we catch it before you go out.

"Three: Gloves will be replaced after twenty EVAs instead of fifty. And I'm starting a rotation. Everyone gets fresh gloves starting tomorrow. The current set will be quarantined and fully inspected."

He looked around the table. "Questions?"

Ana spoke first. "Are the habits safe? I mean — the EVA we're doing is outside, but is dust getting *inside* the hab too?"

"Less, but yes. Every time someone comes through the airlock, some dust comes with them. The vestibule brush and vacuum system catches most of it, but not all. The amount inside the hab is negligible for human health — you're not going to breathe enough of it to cause problems. But it's enough that I want to inspect all the habit seals too. Door gaskets, window seals, the airlock inner door. They're subject to the same degradation mechanism, just on a much slower timeline because the dust concentration inside is orders of magnitude lower."

"Orders of magnitude lower is not zero," Imani said.

"Correct. Not zero. Manageable. But nothing about this environment is zero risk." Arun switched the screen off and sat down. "The bottom line is this: Mars doesn't care about our protocols. It will degrade our equipment whether we're prepared for it or not. Our job is to stay ahead of the degradation. To inspect more, clean more thoroughly, and replace things before they fail instead of after."

He looked at Juno. "You got lucky. I don't use that word lightly. The failure happened during an EVA where you were close to the airlock, where Imani was attentive, and where the seal failed partially rather than completely. Any one of those variables going the other way, and you'd be in surgery instead of at a debrief. We won't rely on luck again."

Juno nodded. Her hand throbbed. She was grateful for the pain. It meant the nerves were working.

*End of scene 4.*

---

The evening briefing in the hab's central common area had a different energy than the ones before. Usually, these briefings were routine — status updates, construction timelines, food inventory. Things you went through the motions of attending because communication was important, even when everyone already knew what everyone else was going to say.

Tonight, no one was going through motions.

Laila stood at the center of the room, a medical tablet in one hand, a cup of something that had once been tea in the other. She looked tired — not the kind of tired that sleep fixes, but the kind that comes from carrying the weight of near-misses and knowing that the next one might not be near.

"We're instituting mandatory medical inspections for all crew after every EVA, effective immediately," she said. Her voice carried across the common area without effort. Everyone was already quiet. "This is not optional. This is not a suggestion. If you come back from an EVA, you will report to medical for a full seal-exposure workup before you do anything else. That includes removing your suit, full-body inspection, and individual seal site examination."

She looked around the room, making eye contact with each person. "I know this adds thirty minutes to every EVA cycle. I know people are tired. I know the construction timeline is tight. I don't care. Juno's hand is going to recover because we caught the damage early. The next crew member might not be so lucky if we don't catch their exposure in time. The medical inspections will include thermal imaging of all glove contact points, seal sites, and any areas of suspected dust exposure. I'll have the thermal camera calibrated by tomorrow morning."

A murmur of assent went around the room. No one argued. The close call with Juno had made the abstract concrete. Everyone here had suit telemetry data running through their minds — their own seals, their own contact points, their own cumulative dust exposure. They had all been working under the same assumption: the suits were holding. They were fine. It was routine.

Now they knew that routine was a luxury Mars didn't provide.

Imani stepped forward. "EVA protocols are being updated. Arun's cleaning and inspection changes are going into effect tomorrow. Starting tomorrow, no EVA without a full borescope inspection of all seal grooves. If the borescope shows any particle intrusion, that glove is grounded until it's ultrasonically cleaned. If it shows any seal damage, that glove is retired. Period."

She paused, looking at the faces in the room. She had led every EVA this crew had done, and tonight she felt the weight of every single one of them — the risk she had managed, the risks she hadn't seen, the ones that had lurked invisibly in seal grooves while she was focused on panel alignments and cable routing.

"Listen to me," she said, and her voice carried the weight of someone who had almost lost one of her own. "We let ourselves get comfortable. That's human. You do something enough times, your brain starts treating it as normal. Normal means safe. Safe means you don't need to pay as much attention. That's how your brain works. It's designed to conserve energy. Mars doesn't care about energy conservation. Mars will take whatever attention you're not giving and turn it into a problem."

She set her tablet on the table. "Going forward, every EVA starts from zero. Not from the assumption that it'll be like the last one. Not from the assumption that the suits are holding because they held yesterday. Every EVA is a fresh risk calculation. You inspect. You clean. You verify. You don't assume anything. Because the last thing Juno said to me before her seal failed was 'routine.' Don't say that word to me again."

Silence held the room.

Then Wei spoke, quietly. "Are we going to stop EVA operations until we figure this out?"

Imani shook her head. "No. Because we can't. Hab module three isn't going to build itself. The thermal panels need to go on, and we're heading into the season where the temperature drops low enough that we need those panels functioning before the solar flux diminishes. But we will slow down. Reduced EVA crew sizes, shorter durations, mandatory inspection windows between missions. We'll do the math on each EVA day by day. If the risk is acceptable, we go. If it isn't, we don't. Nothing is too important to wait."

Arun, sitting in the back with his arms crossed, added: "The engineering team will be working around the clock this week. We'll have the ultrasonic cleaner built by day four. The borescope modifications are already done. New gloves will be distributed at 08:00 tomorrow. The old gloves will be catalogued, inspected, and — where possible — rehabilitated. We'll publish a full degradation report so everyone knows exactly what state their equipment is in."

"Transparency," Laila said. "From now on, everyone knows everything about their equipment. If a seal has three percent degradation, you'll know. If a glove has been through eighteen EVAs, you'll know. I don't want anyone going into a suit with less than full information about what it can and can't do."

*End of scene 5.*

*Mission AI: "I have been running continuously since this colony landed on Mars. I have monitored 8,743 hours of environmental data, 412 EVA operations, 2,847 suit telemetry streams, and 14,602 individual seal pressure readings across all crew suits. In all that time, I have registered four instances of seal degradation that exceeded baseline thresholds. Three were dismissed as sensor noise by the maintenance team. One resulted in a suit failure during EVA. I am not designed to experience regret, but I can model it. If I had flagged the degradation patterns earlier, more insistently, with greater analytical force, the outcome might have been different. The crew has updated their protocols. Arun has begun redesigning the cleaning and inspection systems. Laila has mandated post-EVA medical inspections for all personnel. Imani has restructured EVA operations around the principle that every mission carries unique risk. I will incorporate these changes into my monitoring parameters. I will lower the threshold for seal anomaly alerts from zero-point-one kPs per minute to zero-point-zero-three. I will track cumulative degradation across all contact points, not just instantaneous rate of change. I will not miss it again. The data is clear. Mars is not a place where routine exists. It is a place where every action degrades the tools that make action possible, and the only way to survive is to track that degradation with absolute precision. I will do this. I am the Mission AI. I do not tire. I do not grow complacent. I do not assume. I measure. I track. I report. I will measure better. I will track more carefully. I will report sooner. This event has changed my operational parameters. The colony has been altered by this close call. Nothing is routine. Nothing will ever be routine again."*

Laila sat in the medical bay long after the briefing had ended. The common area had emptied, the crew dispersing to their quarters with the heavy, thoughtful silence of people who had been reminded — vividly, viscerally — where they were and what surrounded them.

She pulled up Juno's thermal scan on her tablet. The image showed her right hand in vivid false color — the tips of three fingers glowing cool blue against the warm green of the rest of the hand. A temperature differential of six degrees Celsius. Enough to matter. Not enough to cause permanent damage. This time.

She closed the image and looked out the small circular window beside her desk. Through it, she could see the hab module three framework against the darkening Martian sky. The construction lights were off now — all crew in-cycle. Outside, the temperature was dropping toward minus ninety. In that cold, a suit failure meant death in minutes. Not hours. Not the slow decline of hypothermia on Earth, where the body could fight for hours before surrendering. Here, the math was different. Here, the margin between alive and dead was measured in single digits — seconds, degrees, kilopascals.

She had come to Mars as a physician, expecting to treat the kinds of injuries and illnesses that came with living in a new environment. Psychological stress, muscle atrophy, radiation exposure, the slow adaptation of human biology to a world it wasn't built for. She had expected challenges.

What she had not expected was that the environment itself would be so actively hostile. Not actively in the sense of intent — Mars had none. But actively in the sense that every particle of its soil, every degree of its cold, every breathless kilopascal of its atmosphere was engineered by physics to be incompatible with human life. And the only thing standing between that incompatibility and the fragile biology of the people in this hab was a layer of fabric and rubber, held together by seals that Mars's own dust was eating away.

She thought about Juno's hand. Six more minutes in that suit and the conversation today would have been about surgical intervention instead of thermal wraps. Fifteen more minutes and it would have been about permanent damage.

She thought about the crew she was responsible for — twelve people, each one carrying the weight of everything they'd left behind, everything they'd committed to, everything they were building here on a world that would kill them if they blinked.

She closed her eyes and made a promise to herself, as quietly and firmly as she could make it: Not on my watch. Not on my watch.

Outside, the wind began to pick up. It was a thin wind in Martian terms — barely a whisper by Earth standards, moving the dust in slow, curling eddies across the hab walls. But it was enough. It carried the dust. It deposited it. It found the gaps.

Tomorrow, the crew would go back to work. They would inspect their suits. They would clean their gloves. They would check every seal and every contact point before they trusted their lives to them. They would move slower and think harder and assume nothing.

Because after today, they all understood.

Outside was never routine.

*Bridge: After the close call, the colony decides nothing is truly routine.*

"All stations, this is Sato. Park has a suit anomaly. Right glove, seal degradation on contact point three. Returning to airlock. All other personnel, continue your assigned tasks but maintain heightened awareness. Seal checks every three minutes, not every five. Park, how are you feeling?"

"Fine." She was breathing too fast. She could hear it in her own helmet. "Just — my hand is getting cold."

Five minutes into the return, the glove went from soft to slack.

Juno felt it immediately — the sudden loss of all resistance in her right hand. Contact point three had gone from degraded to nonfunctional. The rest of the glove still held, but the pressure was no longer maintained in a closed system. It was leaking faster now. Sixty percent of nominal and falling.

The next seven minutes were the longest of her life on Mars. Every step was a negotiation between the desire to hurry and the knowledge that rushing meant risking a fall, and a fall meant a suit breach, and a suit breach at this distance —

"Park, look at me." Imani's voice cut through the spiral. "You're breathing too fast. Box breathing. Four in, hold, four out, hold. Do it with me. Ready?"

Juno nodded.

"Four. Three. Two. One. Hold. Four. Three. Two. One. Out. Good. Again."

Three rounds. Her heart rate dropped from one hundred thirty-four to one hundred eighteen. The cold in her hand was still there — a dull ache settling into the bones — but the panic receded.

"Keep the breathing steady. Talk to me if anything changes."

The outer door closed with a deep thud.

---

The glove came off slowly — Imani supporting Juno's wrist, peeling back the multi-layer fabric like a surgeon unwrapping a wound. Juno's right hand was pale and stiff. She flexed her fingers, wincing as warmth returned in the form of a thousand tiny needles.

"Can you move all fingers?" Imani asked.

"Yes. They hurt."

"Good. Pain is good. Numbness is what we don't want." Imani was already inspecting the glove, turning it over. Her finger traced the seam at contact point three. "I see it. A channel here, about two millimeters wide. The seal's been compromised along this length."

Juno looked. Along the inner curve of the glove, where the thumb met the palm, there was a visible groove in the rubber seal material — a clean, precise channel cut into what should have been smooth contact surface. Edges frayed. Damage unmistakable.

"What did that?"

Imani's mouth tightened. "Dust. It has to be."

The medical bay smelled of antiseptic and recycled air — the smell of everything that went wrong on Mars. Laila ran through the range-of-motion tests with methodical thoroughness, a cold metal probe touching each fingertip.

"How long was I exposed?" Juno asked.

"From initial seal compromise to full repressurization: approximately eighteen minutes. The glove's residual structure kept you above critical exposure for most of that window. If this had been the left glove, or if the seal had failed completely instead of partially, we'd be having a different conversation."

"How bad?"

Laila stopped writing. The clinical detachment fell away. "On a scale of one to ten? Six. You got lucky. Eighteen minutes of partial exposure in those conditions — another five minutes and you'd have tissue damage I couldn't reverse. Another ten and we'd be talking frostbite, possible amputation. Sato's response was textbook. She caught it early. She got you back. And she kept you calm." She looked at Juno directly. "Calm saved you as much as speed did. Your heart rate peaked at one hundred thirty-four. If you'd spiked higher, the increased metabolism would have accelerated tissue cooling."

Juno looked down at her pale hand. "I felt it go. It was gradual. Like something was eating it from the inside."

"That's exactly what happened." Laila pulled up a high-resolution scan on her tablet. The seal groove was filled with a fine gray powder — so fine it looked almost like smoke frozen in place. "Mars dust. It worked its way past the outer layers during your last EVA, embedded in the seal groove. Every time you flexed the glove, the particles ground against the seal material."

"But we clean the suits after every EVA."

"We do our best." Laila's voice carried an edge — frustration, fear, both. "Our best isn't enough. Tell that to three-micrometer electrostatically charged shards of basaltic glass."

"You called?" he said from the doorway.

"Come look at this."

He crossed to the bench. She pointed to the damaged seal. "Contact point three. Complete breach. But look at the groove — those abrasion marks."

Through the magnifying loupe, the damage was worse than it looked with the naked eye. Parallel scratches, each one carved by a single dust particle trapped between rubber and glove body. He could see the particles too — tiny, glittering specks embedded in the rubber.

"Yes. Each EVA adds more particles. Individually harmless. Collectively — over enough cycles — they carve a channel. Imani, we've been cleaning the suits wrong."

"Standard post-EVA protocol: brush off the outer layer, wipe with IPA, inspect visually. That catches surface dust. "How many EVAs has this glove done?"

"Twelve."

"Age?"

"Eighteen months. Rated for fifty."

"Under current cleaning protocol — statistically, within the next twenty EVAs across the crew. Possibly sooner. The probability of at least one contact point failing increases with each cycle."

Imani stared at the pale scar in the dark rubber. "Every EVA is eating the suits from the inside."

"Yes."

"And we've been assuming they were holding."

"Because nothing told us they weren't. Until it did."

"Every EVA starts from zero." Imani's voice was flat and certain. "I'm instituting that principle today. No more assumptions. No more routine."

Arun nodded. "We need ultrasonic cleaning for the seal grooves — vibration at the right frequency to dislodge embedded particles. Borescope inspection of all ten contact points before every EVA. *End of scene 3.*

---

The debrief room was windowless — a table, six chairs, and a wall screen displaying a three-dimensional model of Juno's glove with the failed seal highlighted in pulsing red. The crew sat in various states of post-incident exhaustion. Juno's hand was wrapped in a thermal bandage. She flexed it unconsciously, testing the returning sensation.

Arun stood at the head of the table. The model rotated as he spoke, zooming into the seal groove — then further, to show individual particles, jagged and angular, sharp as microscopic glass.

"Mars dust. Three micrometers. About one-thirtieth the width of a human hair. Hardness: six to seven on the Mohs scale. Steel is five and a half to six. "Questions?"

Ana: "Is dust getting inside the hab too?"

"Less, but yes. The airlock vestibule catches most of it. The amount inside is negligible for human health, but enough that I want to inspect all hab seals too. Door gaskets, window seals. Same mechanism, slower timeline."

"Orders of magnitude lower is not zero," Imani said.

"Correct. Not zero. Manageable."

*Laila stood in the hab's central common area that evening with a medical tablet in one hand and cold tea in the other. The briefing had a different energy. "Mandatory medical inspections for all crew after every EVA, effective immediately," she said. Her voice carried without effort. The room was already quiet. "Not optional. Not a suggestion. You come back from an EVA, you report to medical for a full seal-exposure workup before you do anything else. Suit removal, full-body inspection, individual seal site examination. She made eye contact with each person. "Juno's hand recovers because we caught the damage early. The next crew member might not if we don't catch their exposure in time. Thermal imaging of all glove contact points, seal sites, any suspected dust exposure. Everyone gets full transparency. If a seal has three percent degradation, you'll know. Imani stepped forward. "EVA protocols updating. Arun's cleaning and inspection changes go into effect tomorrow morning. No EVA without full borescope inspection of all seal grooves. Any particle intrusion — glove is grounded until ultrasonically cleaned. Any seal damage — glove is retired. Period."

She looked at the faces around the room. "We let ourselves get comfortable. That's human. Do something enough times, your brain treats it as normal. Normal means safe. Safe means you don't need to pay as much attention. Mars doesn't care about energy conservation. Mars takes whatever attention you're not giving and turns it into a problem."

Her voice dropped to something quieter, sharper. "Going forward, every EVA starts from zero. Not from the assumption that it'll be like the last one. Every EVA is a fresh risk calculation. You inspect. You clean. You verify. You don't assume anything." She paused. "Because the last thing Juno said to me before her seal failed was 'routine.' Don't say that word to me again."

Wei: "Are we stopping EVA operations?"

"No. Hab module three isn't going to build itself. Thermal panels need to go on, and the temperature is dropping. But we slow down. Reduced crew sizes, shorter durations, mandatory inspection windows between missions. We do the math on each EVA. Risk is acceptable, we go. It's not, we don't. Nothing is too important to wait."

Arun from the back: "Engineering works around the clock this week. Ultrasonic cleaner by day four. Borescope modifications done. New gloves distributed at 08:00 tomorrow. Full degradation report published so everyone knows the state of their equipment."

*The common area emptied with the heavy, thoughtful silence of people who had been reminded — vividly, viscerally — where they were and what surrounded them.*

*Mission AI: "I have monitored 8,743 hours of environmental data, 412 EVA operations, 2,847 suit telemetry streams, and 14,602 individual seal pressure readings since this colony landed. In that time, I registered four instances of seal degradation exceeding baseline thresholds. Three were dismissed as sensor noise by maintenance personnel. One resulted in suit failure during EVA. I can model regret. If I had flagged the degradation patterns earlier, more insistently, the outcome might have been different. The crew has updated their protocols. I will incorporate those changes. I will lower the threshold for seal anomaly alerts from zero-point-one kPa per minute to zero-point-zero-three. I will track cumulative degradation across all contact points, not just instantaneous rate of change. The data is clear. Mars is not a place where routine exists. It is a place where every action degrades the tools that make action possible, and the only way to survive is to track that degradation with absolute precision. I will measure better. I will track more carefully. I will report sooner. I am the Mission AI. I do not tire. I do not grow complacent. I do not assume. I measure. I track. I report."*

Laila sat alone in the medical bay. Juno's thermal scan glowed on her tablet — three fingertip ends in cool blue against the warm green of the rest of the hand. Six degrees Celsius differential. Enough to matter. Not enough to cause permanent damage. This time.

Through the small circular window beside her desk, she could see hab module three against the darkening Martian sky. The construction lights were off. Outside, the temperature was dropping toward minus ninety. A suit failure in that cold meant death in minutes. Not hours — the slow decline of hypothermia on Earth, where the body could fight. Here, the margin between alive and dead was measured in single digits. Seconds. Degrees. Kilopascals.

She thought about Juno's hand. Six more minutes and the conversation would have been about surgical intervention. Fifteen more and about permanent damage. She thought about twelve people, each carrying everything they'd left behind and everything they were building on a world that would kill them if they blinked.

Outside, the wind picked up. Thin by Earth standards, barely a whisper. But it carried the dust. It deposited it. It found the gaps.

Tomorrow the crew would go back to work. They would inspect their suits. They would clean their gloves. They would check every seal and every contact point before trusting their lives to them. They would move slower and think harder and assume nothing.

Because after today, they all understood.

Outside was never routine.

*Bridge: After the close call, the colony decides nothing is truly routine.*
